patient.chief_complaint: Monthly 'flashing lights' before a headache — 4 years, now more frequent
patient.hpi:
A 30-year-old Indian woman presented to the neurology clinic with a 4-year history of monthly episodes consisting of 'flashing lights' followed by a severe headache. She describes the visual phenomenon as seeing a bright flickering arc in one side of her vision that expands and then disappears over about 20-25 minutes. She sometimes cannot see clearly on the affected side during this time. The visual disturbance is then followed by a severe unilateral headache (usually right-sided, 7-8/10) with nausea, photophobia, and occasional vomiting lasting 6-8 hours. She has been taking paracetamol (acetaminophen) 1000 mg with only partial relief.

Episodes occur monthly and are particularly associated with her menstrual cycle (occurring within 2-3 days of the start of her period). The frequency has increased from once to twice monthly over the past 3 months after she returned to work from maternity leave. Her sister also has migraines. She is breastfeeding her 6-month-old infant and is not on any contraception. She mentions using low-dose amitriptyline 10 mg for 3 months at a different doctor's office 2 years ago, which helped, but she stopped because she became pregnant. She specifically reports all episodes are identical; there are no 'different' episodes and no neurological symptoms between attacks.
pmh: No hypertension, diabetes, or cardiac disease

family_history: Sister has migraine with aura; no family history of stroke or coagulopathy

social_history.note: Software consultant (returned from maternity leave); breastfeeding 6-month-old; non-smoker; no alcohol currently (breastfeeding); non-smoker

neurological_exam.motor: Motor strength 5/5 all limbs. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.sensory: Sensation intact to light touch and pinprick throughout.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTR 2+ symmetric. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Migraine with typical visual aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1), postpartum exacerbation with menstrually-related pattern

differential.key_features: Aura is stereotyped — this is migraine with aura
Should be considered postpartum; stereotyped aura over 4 years and normal imaging argue against CVST
Requires marked hypertension and encephalopathy — absent here
Acute thunderclap headache and visual field loss — not the pattern here

optimal_actions.action: Take a structured headache/aura history, neurological examination and red-flag review; apply every ICHD-3 1.2 criterion explicitly
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Document attack count; reversible aura modalities; gradual spread; succession; 5–60 minute duration (motor up to 72 hours); unilateral and positive symptoms; relation to headache; medications; examination and red flags

useless_tools.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Routine transthoracic / bubble echocardiogram (PFO screening) is NOT indicated in migraine with aura; PFO-migraine association is controversial and PFO closure does not reduce migraine [Charles_2017]
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential

critical_actions: Counsel on breastfeeding-compatible acute and preventive options [Holland_2012]
contraindicated_actions: Do not start combined oestrogen-progestogen contraception (combined with breastfeeding is doubly contraindicated)
Do not co-administer triptans with ergotamines
key_reasoning_points: Postpartum and menstrual exacerbations of migraine with aura are recognised; the diagnosis is unchanged
Acute and preventive drug selection in breastfeeding follows LactMed / [Holland_2012] guidance

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Anemia may contribute to headache burden but does not cause visual aura; treat anemia as adjunct measure

output.summary: LITERATURE SEARCH: Migraine Treatment During Breastfeeding ACUTE TREATMENT: SAFE FOR BREASTFEEDING: - Acetaminophen (paracetamol): Safe; short half-life - Ibuprofen: Safe (limited transfer to milk; short half-life) - Sumatriptan: COMPATIBLE — low milk transfer (<3% maternal dose); consider pumping and discarding milk for 24 hours after dose as extra precaution (not strictly necessary per WHO) AVOID: - Ergotamine: Contraindicated (vasoconstriction; significant milk transfer) - Aspirin: Avoid (Reye's syndrome risk in infant) - NSAIDs except ibuprofen: Variable safety PREVENTIVE TREATMENT: SAFE: - Amitriptyline 10-25 mg QHS: Limited data but generally considered low risk; LactMed: Probably compatible - Propranolol: Low milk transfer; monitor infant for bradycardia AVOID: - Topiramate: Some transfer to milk; limited neonatal data; generally avoid if breastfeeding - Valproate: Significant milk transfer; avoid CONCLUSION: Add ibuprofen to acetaminophen for acute attacks; sumatriptan compatible with breastfeeding. Amitriptyline 10 mg QHS for prevention (had benefit before). Sumatriptan and ibuprofen compatible with breastfeeding; amitriptyline 10-25 mg QHS safe preventive; avoid topiramate while breastfeeding

DRUG REVIEW — AMITRIPTYLINE DURING BREASTFEEDING Amitriptyline: Low milk-to-plasma ratio (~1:1 but absolute infant dose low at 10-25 mg maternal dose). LactMed: Probably compatible. WHO: Use with caution but acceptable if benefit outweighs risk. RECOMMENDATION: Amitriptyline 10 mg QHS as preventive — prior effective response documented. Discuss with patient regarding acceptable risk during breastfeeding. Monitor infant for sedation. CONCLUSION: Amitriptyline 10 mg QHS compatible with breastfeeding at low doses with monitoring. LITERATURE SEARCH: Postpartum Migraine — Return and Exacerbation KEY FINDINGS:
1. POSTPARTUM MIGRAINE: Migraine commonly worsens in the postpartum period due to hormonal fluctuations (estrogen drop), sleep deprivation, and stress
2. RETURN TO PREPREGNANCY PATTERN: Migraine frequency typically returns to baseline within 3-6 months postpartum
3. BREASTFEEDING: Some evidence breastfeeding is protective against migraine by stabilizing estrogen levels
4. IRON DEFICIENCY ANEMIA: Postpartum anemia may worsen headache burden; treat with iron supplementation
5. SLEEP DEPRIVATION: Major trigger in new mothers; infant sleep training can help CONCLUSION: Postpartum migraine exacerbation explained by hormonal fluctuations, sleep deprivation, and mild anemia. Address all three modifiable factors. Postpartum migraine exacerbation is well-recognised; contributing factors include hormonal fluctuations (oestrogen decline), sleep deprivation, and iron deficiency anaemia; correction of iron deficiency and improved sleep regularity are associated with reduced headache burden in postpartum migraineurs
